title: PDCAT: Preference-Driven Compiler Auto-Tuning
abstract: Compilers are crucial software tools that usually convert programs in high-level languages into machine code. A compiler provides hundreds of optimizations to improve the performance of the compiled code, which are controlled by enabled or disabled optimization flags. However, the vast number of combinations of these flags makes it extremely challenging to select the desired settings for compiler optimization flags (i.e., an optimization sequence) for a given target program. In the literature, many auto-tuning techniques have been proposed to select a desired optimization sequence via different strategies across the entire optimization space. However, due to the huge optimization space, these techniques commonly suffer from the widely recognized efficiency problem. To address this problem, in this paper, we propose a preference-driven selection approach PDCAT, which reduces the search space of optimization sequences through three components. In particular, PDCAT first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation to exclude optimization sequences violating the combined constraints, and then categorizes the optimizations into a common optimization set (whose optimization flags are fixed) and an exploration set containing the remaining optimizations. Finally, within the search process, PDCAT assigns distinct enable probabilities to the explored optimization flags and finally selects a desired optimization sequence. The former two components reduce the search space by removing invalid optimization sequences and fixing some optimization flags, whereas the latter performs a biased search in the search space. To evaluate the performance of the proposed approach PDCAT, we conducted an extensive experimental study on the latest version of the GCC compiler with two widely used benchmarks, cBench and PolyBench. The results show that PDCAT significantly outperforms the four compared techniques, including the state-of-art technique SRTuner. Moreover, each component of PDCAT not only contributes to its performance, but also improves the acceleration performance of the compared techniques.
venue: ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2025)
introduction:
Compilers play an important role in software development [10][11][12]. They usually transform programs written in high-level languages into executable machine code. During this compilation process, compiler optimizations can be applied to achieve various objectives, e.g., reducing the size of compiled code or improving the runtime performance of compiled code. Although GCC provides default optimization settings, such as -O1, -O2, and -O3, these default settings do not often perform well, possibly resulting in larger compiled code or worse runtime performance. Therefore, it is crucial to give a specific compiler optimization setting for a program, particularly for programs that run frequently and whose execution is time-consuming, e.g., Blender, Autodesk Maya, etc. This problem is called the compiler-tuning problem in the literature [1,2,13,17,22,25,33,39,40]. Compiler tuning involves selecting suitable compiler optimizations (i.e., referred to as "flag selection" or "phase selection") and deciding the order in which these optimizations should be applied (i.e., referred to as "phase ordering") [39]. As the latter phase does not apply to most compilers (e.g., GCC), this paper focuses on the former phase.

Common compilers like GCC provide hundreds of optimizations, e.g., loop unrolling and dead code elimination, which are implemented by controlling specific optimization flags (e.g., -floopunroll-and-jam, -fdce, etc.) enabled or disabled. Enabling an optimization flag does not always improve the runtime performance of a program. Due to the large number of optimizations and their exponential combinations, it is difficult for compiler users to understand the impact of each compiler flag on the target program and manually choose compiler optimization flag combinations (i.e., referred to as optimization sequences) for the program. To reduce human effort in setting compiler optimizations, numerous auto-tuning techniques [1,2,13,17,22,25,33,39,40] specifically focusing on flag selection have been proposed in the literature.

The existing auto-tuning techniques regard flag selection as a searching problem, i.e., the combinations of optimization flags compose an optimization space and compiler auto-tuning aims to explore this optimization space through some searching strategy. Following this intuition, various searching strategies, e.g., hill-climbing-based algorithm [2] and genetic algorithm [17,19,26,37], have been proposed, to select a desired optimization sequence. During the searching process, these techniques usually generate numerous optimization sequences, whose corresponding runtime performance of the target program is assessed through compilation and execution. Besides these fixed search strategies, recently some researchers [15,27,28,33] attempted to apply reinforcement learning in the search process, which dynamically adjusts selection strategies during the search process by the rewards calculated based on the runtime performance of existing selected optimization sequences. To sum up, the existing compiler auto-tuning techniques can be characterized by their various search strategies but share the same optimization space. The entire optimization space is huge, and thus exploration in the optimization space tends to be very time-consuming, resulting in unsatisfactory optimization sequences. Therefore, narrowing the optimization space may be a promising direction for compiler auto-tuning because of the reduced searching space.

To narrow the optimization space in compiler auto-tuning, we identify three types of optimization preference based on our understanding: (1) combined optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations that are expected to be used together following the documentation of a compiler;

(2) diverse optimizations, which mean that for any program enabling different optimizations may result in decreased or increased runtime performance; (3) common optimizations, which refers to the set of optimizations whose default setting is given by the compiler. Based on combined optimizations and common optimizations, we remove invalid optimization sequences and ignore the combination among common optimizations, resulting in a reduced optimization space. With our identification of diverse optimization, our search for the desired optimization sequences starts from the optimization sequences whose individual optimization flags have various (not equal) enabling probabilities, resulting in a reduced search space.

In this paper, based on these optimization preferences, we propose a preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique, PDCAT, which first identifies combined optimizations based on compiler documentation, and categorizes the optimizations into two sets, i.e., a set of common optimizations given by the default optimization setting (e.g., -O1) of a compiler and a set composing the remaining optimizations. Then PDCAT explores the combination space of optimizations that fall in the latter set and the optimization sequences violating the combined constraints given by combined optimizations are excluded during the searching process. In particular, within this process, PDCAT first assigns to the explored optimization flags with distinct initial enable probabilities (instead of equal probabilities), which measures how likely an optimization flag is enabled, as well as presents an execution-based adjustment algorithm to modify the enable probabilities of explored flags based on the actual runtime performance for the selected optimization sequences. That is, PDCAT performs a biased search in the reduced optimization space, which is obtained via analyzing the constraints between optimization flags and setting different preferences for different flags.

To evaluate the performance of our approach, we conduct an experiment on the latest widely-used compiler GCC 13.1.0 using two widely used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench. For comparison, we select four representative techniques, including RIO [14], CFSCA [39], CompTuner [40], and state-of-the-art technique SRTuner [33]. For overall effectiveness, PDCAT achieves 5.5%-81.2% acceleration performance over GCC default -O3 optimization setting in all 28 selected cases in 5,000 seconds. Moreover, the optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are significantly better than all compared techniques. In particular, PDCAT achieves the best optimization results in 14 out of 28 cases. For ablation analysis, we construct 14 variants based on PDCAT by varying its three components, and PDCAT achieves a better average acceleration performance than all the variants, which demonstrates the impact of each component of PDCAT. Besides, the acceleration performance of compared techniquesfoot_1 also increases when affiliated with each component of PDCAT.

The contributions of this paper are summarized below.

• A preference-driven compiler auto-tuning technique PDCAT, which first identifies the combined optimizations and categorizes the optimizations into common and explored optimization sets, then conducts a biased search for the explored optimization flags. • An extensive experiment on the latest version of GCC using two widely-used benchmarks cBench and PolyBench, which demonstrates the outperformance of PDCAT as well as its components. • A reproducible package, available in a public repository [38].
experiment:
To evaluate the performance of PDCAT, this experiment is designed to answer two research questions.

• RQ1: Effectiveness. How does PDCAT perform compared to the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning techniques? This RQ investigates the performance of optimization sequences selected by compiler auto-tuning techniques. • RQ2: Ablation analysis. How does each component of PDCAT contribute to the performance? This RQ investigates the impact of each component in PDCAT.

In this experiment, we employ the latest C compiler GCC 13.1.0 as the target compiler. As the existing works [13,39,40], we use the widely used benchmarks cBench [9] and PolyBench [35] as target programs 7 , which cover a wide range of practical functions ranging from 100 to 26,000 lines of code. Table 2 presents the detailed statistics of the target programs, where the "ID" column with C1-C28 denotes the identifiers for the 28 programs from cBench, and P1-P30 denotes the identifiers for the 30 programs from PolyBench.

To validate the effectiveness of our technique, we compare it against four representative baselines:

(1) RIO [14], which is a random iterative optimization technique and is usually taken as a baseline in the existing works [13,39,40], (2) CFSCA [39], which identifies critical optimization flags to speedup the searching process, (3) CompTuner [40], which selects an optimization sequence through multiple-phase learning, and (4) SRTuner [33], which selects an optimization sequence through an interaction process. In particular, CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner are the latest published compiler auto-tuning techniques. SRTuner is the state-of-the-art compiler auto-tuning technique, which has achieved the best auto-tuning performance so far. For a fair comparison, we set a time budget as the termination condition of the compared techniques and compare the optimization sequences generated by these techniques. In particular, we set the time budget to be 1,250, 2,500, and 5,000 seconds, respectively, so as to investigate its influence. Moreover, we repeat each technique five times to alleviate the influence of randomness resulting from the compiler auto-tuning techniques and use the median result to denote the performance of an auto-tuning technique.

We implement PDCAT in Python based on numpy [31]. In particular, in implementing the acquisition of initial enable probabilities of PDCAT, we select 70% of the total programs (i.e., C1-C28 and P1-P30), which amounts to 40 programs, to serve as the initial tuning set 8 . We collect the optimization sequences' performances on these selected programs. To minimize the influence of randomness, we conduct three separate random selections of the initial tuning set and compare the acceleration effects on the remaining test programs after each selection. For each initial tuning program, we randomly generate 500 optimization sequences, balancing data diversity and execution time. In implementing the execution-based tuning algorithm of PDCAT , we set 𝜆 to 0.5, so that to maintain a balance between exploration and exploitation.

In implementing the compared techniques, we directly use their code if they provide a reproducible package (i.e., for CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner); otherwise, we re-implement the technique (i.e., RIO) strictly following the description in the paper. The experiment is performed on a workstation with Intel Xeon CPU E5-2680 v4@2.40GHz with 251G memory and Ubuntu 18.04.6 LTS operating system.

As previous work did [13,33,39,40], we evaluate the runtime performance improvement of a compiler auto-tuning technique by comparing it with the compiler's default optimization settings. Specifically, given that GCC offers several optimization levels such as -O1, -O2, -O3, and -Ofast, we use the -O3 setting as the default for our study, as -O3 is the highest default optimization level of GCC and widely used in existing compiler tuning work [13,33,39,40].

To obtain the runtime performance improvement provided by a compiler auto-tuning technique, we compile any given program 𝑃 using both the selected optimization sequence from the autotuning technique and the default -O3 optimization. This process yields two compiled programs 𝑃 𝑠 and 𝑃 𝑑 . Then we execute both programs and measure the acceleration performance of 𝑃 by dividing (the execution time of 𝑃 𝑑 (i.e., compiled with -O3) -the execution time of 𝑃 𝑠 (i.e., compiled with the selected optimization sequence) × 100% by the execution time of of 𝑃 𝑠 . We use this result to measure compiler auto-tuning techniques.

To answer RQ1, we evaluate the performance of various compiler auto-tuning techniques against the standard -O3 optimization setting. We analyze the speedup ratios across multiple iterations and target programs, highlighting the most and least effective techniques. Table 3 presents the acceleration performances of optimization sequences produced by the compared techniques. Each cell in the table indicates the speedup ratio over -O3 setting, with higher values signifying more effective auto-tuning. For each target program, the best result is highlighted in bold, while the worst is underlined. Due to the iterative selection of different target programs, some are tested multiple times. Thus, for programs selected more than once, Table 3 includes the average acceleration performance across these selections and notes the frequency of each program's selection.

From this table, the acceleration performance of PDCAT varies from 5.1% to 81.2% in 5,000 seconds, indicating that the optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are better than the default -O3 optimization on all target programs. Furthermore, as the time budget increases from 1,250 seconds to 5,000 seconds, the performance of PDCAT presents a corresponding increase.

To further investigate whether PDCAT outperforms the compared baselines, we statistically analyze the experimental results from four perspectives. Firstly, we observe in how many cases where the compared techniques perform worse than PDCAT in different time budgets. Secondly, we explore the best technique by analyzing how many cases a technique achieves the best optimization result and the worst result. Thirdly, we compare the overall acceleration performance of different techniques by analyzing the average acceleration performance for all cases in 5,000 seconds. Finally, we perform significant analysis on PDCAT and other techniques.

We find that most results of the compared baselines (i.e., RIO, OpenTuner, CompTuner and BOCA) are smaller than PDCAT, indicating that given the same time budget the optimization sequences generated by these compared baselines perform worse than PDCAT. Specifically, RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner have worse results than PDCAT on 23/25/25, 19/19/22, 21/20/21 and 18/17/17 programs in 1,250/2,000/5,000 seconds, respectively.

Moreover, we identify the compared auto-tuning technique that achieves the best optimization result (addressed by the font bold) and the worst optimization result (addressed by the underline) for each case and calculate the number of cases where each technique achieves the best optimization results and worst optimization results. The results are given in Table 4. We also discover that PDCAT outperforms the baselines in generating an optimization sequence with good performance in most cases and achieves robust tuning effectiveness on different cases, seldom generating in underperforming optimization sequences. In detail, among the 28 target programs, our proposed PDCAT achieves the best optimization result on 10/11/14 programs in 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while the compared RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieve the best results on only 2/1/1, 5/3/2, 3/5/4 and 8/8/7, respectively. Moreover, PDCAT never achieves the worst results on 28 programs in 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while the compared RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieve the worst results in 18/18/21, 3/3/3, 6/5/3 and 1/2/1, respectively. Furthermore, PDCAT outperforms other techniques in average acceleration performance across all cases, indicating the stability of its tuning performance. Specifically, PDCAT, RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieves an average acceleration performance of 17.0%, 10.7%, 14.5%, 14.3% and 15.6% in the 28 cases in 5,000 seconds, respectively. We perform significance analysis in the 28 cases (with the time budget to be 5,000 seconds) in Tables 3 to compare the acceleration performance of PDCAT and other techniques. We observe that optimization sequences generated by PDCAT are significantly better than all compared techniques. By performing the paired t-test, we calculate the p-values between PDCAT and RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner as 1.5 × 10 -7 , 2.5 × 10 -3 , 5.8 × 10 -5 , and 1.9 × 10 -2 , respectively.

To sum up, our proposed technique PDCAT generates better optimization sequences than the default -O3 optimization of GCC. Moreover, in most cases it outperforms the compared compiler auto-tuning techniques, including the sota work SRTuner, demonstrating that PDCAT is promising.

To learn how PDCAT works, we observe the enable probabilities of different optimization flags during the tuning of program P14. We find that the final enable probability of optimization flag -floop-interchange is 78.2%, while for -ffunction-cse it is only 36.8%. We further examine the source code of P14 and find that P14 has many loop-related operations, and thus it is reasonable for PDCAT to prefer enabling loop-related flag -floop-interchange. To further validate the effects of -floop-interchange and -ffunction-cse, we randomly generate 500 optimization sequences and create another 1,000 sequences by flipping -floop-interchange and -ffunction-cse, respectively, to observe their impact on the acceleration of P14. The results show, with other flags fixed, 379 out of 500 sequences improve the acceleration effect on P14 when -floop-interchange is enabled, whereas only 121 sequences show improved acceleration when -ffunction-cse is enabled, confirming that -floop-interchange should considered be enabled during the tuning of P14.

To answer RQ2, we construct 14 variants (i.e., 4 major variants, 10 secondary variants) by removing or replacing each component individually, or integrating some components with existing techniques. Variants that remove components of PDCAT are considered as major variants, while those that modify components of PDCAT or apply components of PDCAT to other techniques are considered as secondary variants. We analyze the contribution of each component of PDCAT by comparing the acceleration performance between PDCAT and these variants in 1,250, 2,500, and 5,000 secondsfoot_10 .

Without initial enable probabilities acquisition phase. To investigate the contribution of initial enable probabilities acquisition phase, we set the initial enable probabilities of the explored flags randomly rather than obtaining them by the tuning data, resulting in a major variant of PDCAT (denoted as 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 ). Table 5 presents the acceleration performances of optimization sequences produced by PDCAT and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 on the selected test programs, with better results highlighted in bold. Due to the random selection, some programs, e.g., C1, C2, do not appear in the table as initial tuning programs.

We observe that PDCAT outperforms 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 in most cases, confirming the effectiveness of the initial enable probabilities acquisition for flag's enable probabilities in PDCAT. In particular, PDCAT achieves better acceleration performance in 15/16/15 of the 18 cases in 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 only achieves better acceleration performance on 3/2/3 of the 18 cases. In particular, PDCAT achieves an average acceleration performance of 16.5% in the 18 cases in 5,000 seconds, while 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 achieves an average acceleration performance of 13.2%. In a relatively short period of time (i.e., 1,250s and 2,500s), 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 performs worse, indicating that the random initial enable probabilities, compared to those obtained from tuning data, may reduce the overall effectiveness of the technique.

Number of initial tuning programs. Moreover, in implementing PDCAT in this evaluation, we set the number of initial tuning programs to be 40. To investigate the influence of this number, we implement another two PDCAT whose numbers of initial tuning programs are 10 and 20, and call these two secondary variants as 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 10 and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 20 .

We find the size of the initial tuning program set impacts the final tuning results, when the set is larger, the initial enable probabilities obtained are more accurate, leading to better overall acceleration performances. 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 10 and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 20 achieves an average acceleration performances of 13.8% and 14.7%, while PDCAT achieves an average acceleration performance of 16.5% and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝐼𝑛𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 achieves an average acceleration performance of 13.2% in 18 cases in 5,000 seconds, respectively.

Then we generate optimization sequences according to the fixed enable probabilities under constraints, resulting in a major variant of PDCAT (denoted as 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝑇𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 ). Due to the random selection, some programs, e.g., C1, C2, do not appear in the table as initial tuning programs.

We find that 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝑇𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 performs significantly worse than PDCAT, confirming the effectiveness of tuning on program in PDCAT. From Table 6, 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑁 𝑜𝑇𝑢𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 only achieves better acceleration performance on 3/3/4 of the 18 cases and average acceleration performance of 14.2% in 5,000 seconds, while PDCAT achieves better acceleration performance in 15/15/14 of the 18 cases and average acceleration performance of 16.5% in 5,000 seconds. flags and treat all of the flags as explored flags, resulting in a major variant of PDCAT (denoted as 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 ). Table 8 presents the acceleration performances of optimization sequences produced by PDCAT and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 on the selected test programs, with better results highlighted in bold.

From Table 8, 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 achieves better acceleration performance on 5/4/5 of the 18 cases and an average acceleration performance of 14.9% in 5,000 seconds, which are worse than PDCAT, indicating the contribution of identifying a common optimization set.

For some programs, 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 achieves better acceleration performances than PDCAT, although the former searches across the entire optimization space. We suspect that 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 discovers newer optimization areas during the search, resulting in better optimization sequences. Note that the default -O1 optimization in compilers does not necessarily lead to performance acceleration 10 , which may be the reason for this observation. Different common optimization sets. Moreover, to verify the impact of common optimization set, we use GCC default -O2/-O3 optimization as common optimization set and the remaining flags as explored flags, resulting in two secondary variants of PDCAT (denoted as 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑂2 and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑂3 ).

The average acceleration effects achieved by 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑂2 and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑂3 in 18 cases are 14.7% and 12.6% in 5,000 seconds, respectively. Compared to PDCAT and 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝐴𝑙𝑙𝐸𝑥𝑝 , 𝑃𝐷𝐶𝐴𝑇 𝑂3 's performance declines significantly. GCC 13.1.0's default -O1 optimization includes 47 optimization flags, -O2 optimization includes 98 optimization flags (includes all optimization flags of -O1), and -O3 includes 111 optimization flags (includes all optimization flags of -O2). We suspect this is due to too few explored flags, resulting in too small an optimization space.

Common optimization set for other techniques. Additionally, to verify the effectiveness of the common optimization set for the other techniques, we modify the compared techniques (i.e., CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner) by holding some of the optimization flags fixed as the default -O1 optimization, and exploring the remaining flags following their original way, resulting in three secondary variants (denoted as 𝐶𝐹𝐶𝑆𝐴 𝑂1 , 𝐶𝑜𝑚𝑝𝑇𝑢𝑛𝑒𝑟 𝑂1 , and 𝑆𝑅𝑇𝑢𝑛𝑒𝑟 𝑂1 ). The results show that after using common optimizations, the performance of CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner all improve, achieving acceleration performances of 14.1%, 13.8%, and 15.4% in 5,000 seconds, respectively.

Based on the results above, determining how to select the appropriate explored flags to achieve the best balance between exploration and exploitation remains a challenge that we need to address in the future.
task_title: Efficient Compiler Auto-Tuning for Optimization Flag Selection
background: Compilers translate high-level code into machine code, providing numerous optimization flags (e.g., -floop-unroll-and-jam, -fdce) to improve runtime performance or code size. For a given program, choosing a near-optimal combination of flags (an optimization sequence) is challenging because of the exponential number of possible flag combinations. Manually tuning flags is infeasible, so automatic compiler auto-tuning techniques have been proposed. Most existing techniques treat flag selection as a search problem, exploring the full optimization space using strategies like genetic algorithms or reinforcement learning. However, due to the vast space, exploration is time-consuming and often yields only modest improvements over default settings. A promising direction is to reduce the search space so that exploration can be more efficient while still discovering high-performance sequences.
research_question: How can compiler auto-tuning efficiently select optimization flag sequences that achieve better runtime performance than default compiler optimization levels, given a limited time budget?

datasets.name: cBench
datasets.description: A collection of 28 C programs with varying computational characteristics, ranging from 100 to 26,000 lines of code.

datasets.name: PolyBench
datasets.description: A benchmark suite of 30 computational kernels for polyhedral optimization, written in C.

baselines.name: CFSCA
baselines.reference: Critical Flag Selection for Compiler Auto-tuning (CFSCA) [39]

metrics.name: Speedup ratio over -O3
metrics.definition: (execution_time_O3 - execution_time_selected) / execution_time_selected * 100%. A higher value indicates better runtime performance.

rqs: RQ1: How does the runtime performance improvement of the auto-tuning technique compare to the baseline techniques across different time budgets?
RQ2: How do different design choices within the auto-tuning technique affect its overall effectiveness?
experiment_setup.target_subject: C programs from cBench (28 programs) and PolyBench (30 programs) benchmarks, with varying code size and computational patterns, running on GCC 13.1.0.
experiment_setup.constraints: The search time budget per program is limited to 1250, 2500, and 5000 seconds. Each technique is executed 5 times per program to account for randomness, and the median speedup is reported. The compiler used is GCC 13.1.0. Experiments are conducted on a workstation with Intel Xeon CPU E5-2680 v4, 251GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04.

feasibility_notes: Both benchmarks are publicly available and widely used. Reproducing the full experiment requires extensive compilation and execution runs; each technique-program-budget combination requires multiple runs, totaling hundreds of invocations. With 58 programs, 4 baselines, and 3 budgets, the total experiment may require several days of compute time on a powerful workstation. The environment needs GCC 13.1.0 and a Linux system. Randomness in the auto-tuning process increases the computational burden.
